question.text: Decarboxylation of all six possible forms of diaminobenzoic acids <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi><mn>6</mn></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">H</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msub><mfenced><msub><mi>NH</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>COOH</mi></math> yields three products <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>. Three acids give a product '<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">A</mi></math>', two acids gives a product '<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">B</mi></math>' and one acid give a product '<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>'. The melting point of product '<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>' is

solution.text:
C is a para isomer.

The melting point of para-isomer is comparatively higher than the corresponding  ortho and meta-isomers , because of more symmetrical nature; it fits into crystal lattice more readily and so, close packing of molecules in crystal lattice increases the intermolecular force of attraction between molecules.

Hence C has highest melting point that is 142 °C
